The wind at the edge of the world did not blow; it screamed. It was a sound that lived in the marrow of the stone, a constant, high-pitched keen that vibrated through the soles of Elias Thorne’s boots as he climbed the final spiral of the tower.

Elias was Lighthouse Keeper #0.

The number was not a rank, nor a mistake. It was an origin. While the other keepers on the coast—Keepers #1 through #14—were assigned to specific posts based on trade routes and seasonal shifts, #0 was a position that existed before the map was drawn. He was the First. He was the Last. And he was alone.

The lighthouse itself, known locally as The Needle, was not a building in the traditional sense. It was a spire of black basalt, rising from a jagged shelf of rock that jutted out into the churning gray Atlantic. It had no door at the base, only a seam in the stone that opened with a hand carved into the rock. The light at the top was not a lamp, but a lens the size of a carriage wheel, filled with something that looked like liquid starlight.

Elias reached the top. The wind died here, replaced by a silence so profound it felt like pressure. He stepped through the seam into the lantern room. The glass was thick, curved, and cold. In the center of the room stood the mechanism: a massive brass armature that held the lens.

"Report," Elias said to the empty room. His voice sounded too loud, too human.

The mechanism hummed. A low, resonant thrum that traveled up through the floorboards.

# The Keeper of the Void

The lighthouse was not on a map. It stood on a jagged promontory of black basalt, a needle piercing the gray, churning sky, at the very edge of the charted world. The cliffs below were slick with salt spray and ancient moss, and the sea beyond was not merely water; it was a living, breathing entity that seemed to stare back at the tower with an intelligence that was just shy of human.

This was Lighthouse Zero.

And this was Elias Thorne, its Keeper.

Elias was seventy-two years old, though he looked older. His face was a topographical map of wind and sun, carved into deep lines by decades of exposure to the elements. His hair was white as the foam of the breaking waves, and his eyes, behind thick, cracked spectacles, held a perpetual squint, as if he were always trying to focus on something far in the distance. He was a small man, wiry and stooped, who moved with a deliberate, creaking slowness that belied the strength required to climb the four hundred steps of the spiral staircase every morning.

Every morning, he climbed. Every evening, he descended. And every night, he lit the light.

The routine was absolute. It was the only thing that kept the world from unraveling.
